questions.prompt: Which three building blocks does a computer need to store a location on the Earth?
choices: A datum, a coordinate system, and a projection
An address, a ZIP code, and a county
A raster, a vector, and a table
A scale bar, a legend, and a north arrow
questions.explain: The datum models the Earth, the coordinate system lays a grid on it, and the projection flattens it.

questions.prompt: Why are coordinates better than landmarks for storing location in a computer?
choices: They are unambiguous and easy to store, compare, and measure between
They are easier for people to remember
They never change when the datum changes
They work without any reference system
questions.explain: A landmark only helps people who know it; a pair of coordinates means one place to anyone with the same reference system.

questions.prompt: The science of measuring the Earth's size, shape, orientation, and gravity is:
questions.explain: Every coordinate rests on a geodetic model of the Earth.

questions.prompt: How did Eratosthenes estimate the Earth's circumference?
choices: From the angle of noon shadows in two cities a known distance apart
From the shape of the Moon during an eclipse
By measuring the height of mountains
questions.explain: A 7.2° shadow is 1/50 of a circle, so he multiplied the distance between Syene and Alexandria by 50.

questions.prompt: The Earth's shape is best approximated by:
choices: An ellipsoid, flattened at the poles
An ellipsoid, flattened at the Equator
questions.explain: Because it spins, the Earth bulges at the Equator: about 6,378 km to the Equator and 6,357 km to the poles.

questions.prompt: The flattening of the Earth is about 1 / ___ .
On an ellipsoid, the semi-major axis runs from the center to:
questions.explain: The semi-major axis, a, is the longer one; the semi-minor axis, b, runs to a pole.

questions.prompt: What does a geodetic datum do?
choices: It fixes an ellipsoid and pins it to the real Earth
It flattens the globe onto a map
It stores the attributes of a feature
questions.explain: Change the datum and the same latitude and longitude point to a slightly different place on the ground.

questions.prompt: The brass disks set in bridges and sidewalks by the National Geodetic Survey are:
questions.explain: Thousands of surveyed control points make a datum real on the ground.

questions.prompt: Which datum does GPS use?
questions.explain: WGS84 is the World Geodetic System of 1984. In North America it is within a meter or two of NAD83.

questions.prompt: Which datum used the Clarke 1866 ellipsoid and a single origin point in Kansas?
questions.explain: NAD83 replaced it, using the GRS80 ellipsoid. Shifts between the two can be tens of meters or more.

questions.prompt: Lines of latitude are called:
questions.explain: Parallels run east–west, parallel to the Equator.

questions.prompt: Lines of longitude, which run from pole to pole, are called:
questions.explain: Meridians meet at the poles.

questions.prompt: Why was the Prime Meridian's location agreed on at a conference in 1884?
choices: Unlike the Equator, 0° longitude has no natural place
Greenwich is at the center of the Earth
It marks where the datum starts
questions.explain: The poles and Equator come from the Earth's rotation; the starting meridian had to be chosen.

questions.prompt: Which goes all the way around the Earth through 360°?
questions.explain: Longitude runs 180° east and 180° west. Latitude runs 90° north and 90° south: 180° in all.

questions.prompt: The network of parallels and meridians drawn on a map is the:
questions.explain: Match its interval to the scale, and keep its lines thin and light.

questions.prompt: Convert −104.54° to degrees, minutes, and seconds. How many minutes?
Convert 35° 30′ 0″ N to decimal degrees.
In decimal degrees, a negative longitude means:
questions.explain: Negative means south latitude or west longitude. North Carolina's longitudes are all negative.

questions.prompt: Why can't you convert a distance in degrees to kilometers with a single factor?
choices: A degree of longitude shrinks toward the poles
Degrees are only used at sea
A degree of latitude changes with the datum
questions.explain: A degree of longitude is about 111 km at the Equator, about 90 km in Chapel Hill, and zero at the poles.

questions.prompt: Put the layers of a projection in order, from the bottom (the real Earth) up.
questions.explain: Each layer rests on the one below; change a lower layer and everything above it shifts.

questions.prompt: Every map projection distorts at least one of:
questions.explain: You can't flatten the globe without stretching or tearing it.

questions.prompt: Which property does the Mercator projection preserve?
choices: Local shape and angles (it is conformal)
questions.explain: That made it ideal for navigation, but it badly inflates areas near the poles.

questions.prompt: On a Mercator map, Greenland looks about as big as Africa. In reality, Africa is about how many times larger?
questions.explain: Greenland is about the size of the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

questions.prompt: You want to compare forest area across countries. Which kind of projection should you use?
questions.explain: Equal-area projections, such as Albers or Mollweide, keep relative sizes true.

questions.prompt: A projection can be both conformal and equal-area.
questions.explain: No projection can be both. Compromise projections, such as Robinson, preserve nothing exactly.

questions.prompt: Where is the scale exactly true on a secant projection?
choices: Along the standard lines, where the map surface cuts the globe
At the edges of the map
questions.explain: Distances shrink between the standard lines and stretch outside them.

questions.prompt: North Carolina's State Plane zone uses which projection, because the state is wide from east to west?
questions.explain: East–west zones use Lambert Conformal Conic; north–south zones use Transverse Mercator. NC is EPSG:32119.

questions.prompt: Which sf function changes a layer's coordinates to a new CRS?
questions.explain: st_crs() reports the CRS; st_set_crs() only changes the label, not the coordinates.

questions.prompt: What is EPSG:4326?
questions.explain: EPSG codes identify coordinate reference systems. 32119 is NC State Plane in meters.

questions.prompt: Convert 79° 3′ 21″ W to decimal degrees and store it in `dd`. Remember the sign.
questions.solution:
deg <- 79
min <- 3
sec <- 21
dd <- -(deg + min / 60 + sec / 3600)
questions.explain: 79 + 3/60 + 21/3600 = 79.0558, and west is negative.

questions.prompt: A degree of longitude is about `111.32 * cos(latitude)` km, with the latitude in radians. Store the length of a degree of longitude at 36° N in `km`.
questions.explain: Multiply degrees by pi / 180 to get radians. The answer is about 90 km.
